subject: Economics
description: Covers Direct/Indirect, CBDT/CBIC, GST Amendment, Proportional tax, GST Council, Buoyancy, and Cess.

questions.stem: In India, which authority administers the collection of Direct Taxes such as Income Tax and Corporate Tax?

options.option_text: Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)
Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)
Enforcement Directorate (ED)
Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN)

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) is the statutory authority functioning under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963. It deals with matters relating to the levy and collection of all direct taxes in India (primarily Income Tax and Corporate Tax). It operates under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.
DECOY BUSTING: CBIC handles indirect taxes (Customs, Central Excise, Service Tax, and GST). The ED investigates economic crimes like money laundering (PMLA) and foreign exchange violations (FEMA). The GSTN is an IT company that provides the technological backbone for the GST portal.
EXAM INSIGHT: Understanding the division between CBDT and CBIC is fundamental for economics and polity questions. The Chairman of CBDT is the senior-most IRS (Income Tax) officer in India.

questions.stem: Which constitutional amendment act paved the way for the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India?

options.option_text: 101st Amendment Act, 2016
99th Amendment Act, 2014
103rd Amendment Act, 2019
105th Amendment Act, 2021

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act of 2016 introduced Article 246A, which gave concurrent powers to the Centre and States to make laws with respect to GST. This was a monumental shift in India's federal structure, creating a unified national market ("One Nation, One Tax").
DECOY BUSTING: 
- 99th Amendment: National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), which was struck down by the Supreme Court.
- 103rd Amendment: 10% EWS Quota.
- 105th Amendment: Restored the power of State governments to identify Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs).
EXAM INSIGHT: GST replaced a complex web of indirect taxes including Central Excise Duty, Service Tax, State VAT, and Entry Tax. It was officially launched at midnight on July 1, 2017.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Under the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime, which of the following items is completely EXEMPT from GST (i.e., kept outside its purview)?

options.option_text: Alcohol for human consumption
Gold and precious metals
Restaurants and catering services
Luxury cars and SUVs

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Article 366(12A) of the Constitution explicitly defines GST as any tax on the supply of goods or services or both, EXCEPT taxes on the supply of the alcoholic liquor for human consumption. Thus, alcohol is constitutionally outside GST, and states continue to levy their own massive State Excise duties on it (a huge source of state revenue).
DECOY BUSTING: Five petroleum products (crude oil, diesel, petrol, natural gas, ATF) are currently outside GST, but they can be brought under it later if the GST Council decides. Gold is taxed under GST at a special rate of 3%. Restaurants usually attract 5% GST. Luxury cars attract the highest 28% slab plus a compensation cess.
EXAM INSIGHT: State governments heavily lobbied to keep alcohol and petrol out of GST to preserve their fiscal autonomy, as these two items generate the bulk of state tax revenues.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a 'Proportional Tax' system?

options.option_text: The tax rate remains the same regardless of the income level of the taxpayer
The tax rate increases as the income of the taxpayer increases
The tax rate decreases as the income of the taxpayer increases
The tax is levied based strictly on the geographical location of the taxpayer

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: In a proportional tax system (often called a 'flat tax'), everyone pays the exact same percentage of their income, regardless of how much they earn. For example, if the rate is 10%, a person earning 10,000 pays 1,000, and a person earning 1,000,000 pays 100,000. 
DECOY BUSTING: 
- "Tax rate increases as income increases" = Progressive Tax (like India's Income Tax slabs). This is favored for reducing income inequality.
- "Tax rate decreases as income increases" = Regressive Tax. Indirect taxes like GST are considered regressive because a Rs 100 tax on a shirt takes a larger percentage of a poor person's income than a rich person's income.
EXAM INSIGHT: Corporate Tax in India largely functions as a proportional tax (a flat percentage on profits), though there are varying rates based on company turnover or manufacturing status.

questions.stem: What is the primary function of the GST Council as established under Article 279A of the Indian Constitution?

options.option_text: To make recommendations to the Union and States on GST rates, exemptions, and threshold limits
To physically collect and distribute GST revenue to the respective state treasuries
To audit the tax filings of large multinational corporations operating in India
To resolve disputes between the CBDT and CBIC regarding direct vs indirect tax jurisdictions

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The GST Council is the apex decision-making body for GST. It is a joint forum of the Centre and the States, chaired by the Union Finance Minister. Its mandate is to recommend GST rates, decide which goods/services are exempt, set threshold limits, and frame rules. It exemplifies 'cooperative federalism'.
DECOY BUSTING: The physical collection is done through the GSTN portal and CBIC/State authorities, not the Council itself. Audits are done by tax officers. CBDT vs CBIC disputes are internal Ministry of Finance matters, totally unrelated to the GST Council.
EXAM INSIGHT: Voting in the GST Council is carefully balanced: The Centre's vote has a weightage of 1/3rd, while the combined States' votes have a weightage of 2/3rds. Every decision requires a 3/4th majority. This means neither the Centre alone nor the States alone can pass a resolution.

questions.stem: Which term describes the phenomenon where the tax revenue collected by the government automatically increases at a faster rate than the growth in the country's GDP, without any change in tax rates?

options.option_text: Tax Buoyancy
Tax Evasion
Fiscal Drag
Tax Arbitrage

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Tax buoyancy measures the responsiveness of tax revenue growth to GDP growth. If GDP grows by 10% and tax revenue grows by 15% (without the government hiking the tax rates), the tax buoyancy is 1.5. A buoyancy greater than 1 means the tax system is highly efficient and captures the expanding economy effectively (often through better compliance or formalization).
DECOY BUSTING: Tax elasticity is similar but measures the effect of deliberate changes in tax rates. Fiscal drag occurs when inflation pushes taxpayers into higher income tax brackets, increasing government revenue without real income growth. Tax evasion is the illegal non-payment of taxes.
EXAM INSIGHT: Post-demonetization and the implementation of GST, the Indian government frequently cites improving "tax buoyancy" as proof that the informal economy is formalizing and tax compliance is increasing.

questions.stem: A 'Cess' in the Indian taxation system is different from a normal tax because:

options.option_text: It is levied for a specific purpose, and the revenue generated must strictly be spent on that purpose
It is only imposed on imported goods crossing international borders
It is collected exclusively by State Governments to fund panchayats
It is a voluntary contribution made by wealthy individuals instead of paying income tax

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: A cess is a "tax on tax," levied by the government for a very specific purpose. Unlike normal tax revenues (which go into the Consolidated Fund of India and can be spent on anything), the revenue from a cess is ring-fenced. It must first be credited to the CFI and then transferred to a dedicated fund (e.g., the Education Cess goes to the Prarambhik Shiksha Kosh). 
DECOY BUSTING: Border taxes are Customs Duties. A 'Surcharge' is also a tax on tax, but unlike a cess, surcharge revenue can be used for any general purpose. Voluntary contributions are donations, not taxes.
EXAM INSIGHT: A crucial constitutional point often asked in UPSC: The Centre DOES NOT have to share the revenue from cesses and surcharges with the State governments (they are excluded from the divisible pool decided by the Finance Commission). This is a major grievance of state governments.

questions.stem: In public finance terminology used in Indian taxation, the 'impact' of a tax refers to which of the following?

options.option_text: The final economic burden that falls on the last person in the supply chain
The initial legal liability to pay tax at the point of its first imposition
The revenue generated by the tax expressed as a percentage of national income
The cascading effect caused by levying tax on already-taxed goods or services

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'tax impact' (or statutory incidence) denotes the point where the tax is first legally imposed — i.e., who must hand over the money to the government. Option A describes 'tax incidence', which is where the economic burden ultimately rests after shifting through price mechanisms. Candidates routinely confuse the two; incidence is the final burden, impact is the first legal touch-point.

questions.stem: Article 276 of the Indian Constitution empowers state legislatures to levy taxes on professions, trades and employment. After the Constitution (Sixtieth Amendment) Act, 1988, the ceiling on such tax per person per year was fixed at:

options.option_text: ₹1,000 per annum — the figure set in the original 1950 Constitution
₹2,500 per annum — revised upward from the earlier ₹250 per annum limit
₹5,000 per annum — aligned with post-liberalisation wage revision norms
₹3,000 per annum — as amended by the Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976

questions.explanation: B is correct. The original Article 276 capped professional tax at ₹250 per annum; the 60th Constitutional Amendment (1988) raised this to ₹2,500, where it still stands. Option D is a fabricated amendment link — the 42nd Amendment dealt with administrative and emergency provisions, not professional tax. Option C invents a figure. Many candidates confuse the pre- and post-amendment figures.

questions.stem: Under the GST framework, the Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM) shifts the tax payment obligation from the supplier to the recipient of supply. Which of the following transactions would correctly attract RCM?

options.option_text: Interstate sale of taxable goods between two GST-registered manufacturers
Procurement of legal services from a senior advocate by a registered business
Import of goods by an unregistered individual exclusively for personal consumption
Export of taxable goods by a registered exporter under zero-rated supply rules

questions.explanation: B is correct. The GST law specifically lists legal services provided by an advocate (including a senior advocate) to a business entity as a notified category under RCM — the business recipient must pay GST directly to the government, not the advocate. Option A describes a normal forward-charge B2B transaction. Option C is not RCM because personal-consumption imports by unregistered individuals are covered under a different levy. Option D (zero-rated exports) attract nil GST, making RCM irrelevant.

questions.stem: India enters into Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) with foreign countries to prevent the same income from being taxed in both jurisdictions. Under the Income Tax Act, 1961, which provision grants the Central Government this treaty-making power?

options.option_text: Section 90 — agreements with foreign governments to grant relief from double taxation
Section 80C — deductions available to individuals for specified savings instruments
Section 115JB — provisions for computing Minimum Alternate Tax on company book profits
Section 195 — mandatory deduction of tax at source from payments made to non-residents

questions.explanation: A is correct. Section 90 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 empowers the Central Government to enter into DTAAs with foreign countries or specified territories; Section 90A further covers agreements adopted by notified associations. Option D (Section 195) is a common distractor because it also involves non-residents and TDS, but it is a withholding provision, not the treaty-authorisation clause. Options B and C are unrelated domestic deduction/computation provisions.

questions.stem: Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) was introduced to ensure companies reporting large book profits cannot escape taxation through heavy deductions. On which base is MAT liability computed under Section 115JB of the Income Tax Act?

options.option_text: Taxable income arrived at after all permissible deductions under the Income Tax Act
Book profits as per the profit and loss account prepared under the Companies Act
Gross total receipts of the company before deducting any operating expenditure
Net worth of the company recorded on the last day of the relevant financial year

questions.explanation: B is correct. MAT is levied at a specified rate (currently 15% plus surcharge and cess) on 'book profits' — the net profit shown in the P&L account prepared as per the Companies Act, with certain prescribed additions and deductions. Option A describes the normal Income Tax computation; MAT exists precisely because that computation could result in zero or negligible tax for profit-making companies. Options C and D are fabricated bases not used in MAT.

questions.stem: India's General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) empowers tax authorities to deny benefits of arrangements that qualify as 'Impermissible Avoidance Arrangements'. Under the GAAR guidelines, below what aggregate tax benefit threshold can GAAR provisions NOT be invoked against an arrangement?

options.option_text: Aggregate tax benefit falling below ₹1 crore in the relevant financial year
Aggregate tax benefit falling below ₹3 crore in the relevant financial year
Aggregate tax benefit falling below ₹5 crore in the relevant financial year
Aggregate tax benefit falling below ₹10 crore in the relevant financial year

questions.explanation: B is correct. GAAR (applicable from AY 2018-19) includes a de minimis safe harbour: if the aggregate tax benefit in the arrangement is less than ₹3 crore (₹30 million), GAAR cannot be invoked. This threshold prevents harassment of small transactions. Options A, C, and D are plausible round-number distractors — ₹5 crore is a common misremembered figure. Candidates must also recall that GAAR requires both (i) the main purpose being tax benefit AND (ii) at least one of four conditions (lack of arm's length, abuse of law, lack of commercial substance, non-bona fide manner).

questions.stem: In public finance analysis of the Indian tax system, 'tax buoyancy' and 'tax elasticity' both measure how tax revenues respond to GDP growth. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?

options.option_text: Buoyancy strips out discretionary policy changes; elasticity captures both automatic and policy-driven revenue shifts
Elasticity strips out discretionary policy changes; buoyancy captures both automatic and policy-driven revenue shifts
Buoyancy is computed only for direct taxes; elasticity is computed only for indirect taxes in Indian fiscal analysis
Elasticity is the ratio of nominal GDP growth to tax growth; buoyancy relates tax growth to the prevailing price level

questions.explanation: B is correct. Tax elasticity measures the pure, built-in responsiveness of tax revenue to GDP — discretionary changes (new levies, rate changes, exemptions removed) are excluded by adjusting the data. Tax buoyancy uses actual observed revenue without stripping out policy changes, so it reflects the combined effect of both automatic growth and deliberate policy action. Option A has the definitions reversed — the most common error. Options C and D are fabricated distinctions not used in standard public finance methodology.
